text: Equal temperament is a compromise — every interval except the octave is slightly wrong, but the wrongness is distributed so evenly that no key sounds worse than any other.

Just intonation tunes intervals using pure integer ratios derived from the harmonic series. A just perfect fifth is 3:2, and it sounds noticeably cleaner than its equal-tempered counterpart — no beating, just stillness.

The Pythagorean comma is what happens when you stack twelve perfect fifths and expect to land back at your starting pitch. You don't. You overshoot by about 23.46 cents, and that gap is the mathematical proof that pure tuning and free modulation cannot coexist.

There's something philosophically uncomfortable about equal temperament — we've collectively agreed to use a tuning system where every chord is technically out of tune, because the alternative was worse for composers who wanted to move between keys.

Microtonality isn't just about using more notes — it's about asking which of the twelve we use are actually arbitrary. If you've always assumed 12-EDO is natural, a piece in 31-EDO dismantles that assumption one interval at a time.

Harry Partch didn't adapt his musical ideas to available instruments — he built instruments capable of playing his 43-tone just intonation scale, because no existing instrument could do what he needed. The Chromelodeon, the Quadrangularis Reversum — these are acoustics made physical.

The Arabic maqam system doesn't just add quarter-tones as ornaments. The quarter-tone is a structural pitch, with a specific role in the melodic grammar of a given maqam. Treating it as an inflection misses the point.

Meantone tuning was an early attempt to fix Pythagorean intonation's worst fifths by making all fifths slightly flat, allowing the major thirds to be nearly pure. It worked — until you hit the wolf interval.
The wolf interval is the tuning system's failure mode made audible: the one fifth (or fourth) that bears the accumulated error from every other corrected interval. In meantone tuning, it howls.

What would harmonic purity actually mean for a solo piano piece? The pianist can't retune mid-performance. Harmonic purity is structurally available to string quartets and choirs, but the piano is built around the equal-tempered compromise.

Just intonation and equal temperament aren't just tuning systems — they represent different answers to what music is for. One says music should reflect the physics of vibrating strings. The other says music should serve compositional freedom.

24-EDO divides the octave into 24 equal parts, giving you all the standard semitones plus a quarter-tone between each. It's the most common microtonal system in use because it's the smallest extension of 12-EDO that remains comprehensible to Western-trained ears.
The Pythagorean comma shows up not just in music theory but in the history of keyboard design — the whole story of how temperament evolved is an engineering problem as much as an aesthetic one.

In just intonation, the major third above A is not the same pitch as the minor fourth below D, even though both are nominally C#. This is the syntonic comma, and it's why fixed-pitch just intonation keyboards become a forest of split keys.

La Monte Young's drone works are often cited as just intonation in practice — the intervals are held long enough that the difference between pure and tempered becomes physically perceptible as beating or its absence.

Maqam Rast doesn't just use a pitch between E and Eb — it uses that pitch in a specific melodic context where it resolves in a particular direction. The structural function is inseparable from the microtonal placement.

I keep wondering if Western listeners hear microtonal music as 'out of tune' because quarter-tones are genuinely dissonant or simply because we've been trained to expect 12-EDO. Probably both, in different proportions depending on the listener.

Equal temperament wasn't universally adopted until the 19th century. Baroque keyboard music was performed in a variety of well temperaments — each key had a distinct character because each was tuned slightly differently.

The wolf interval is an interesting case: the tuning system hides its error everywhere else and then dumps it all in one place. The result is an interval so badly out of tune that it was traditionally avoided at all costs in composition.

72-EDO is championed by some microtonal theorists because it contains excellent approximations of both 12-EDO and just intonation intervals — it subsumes both systems without being reducible to either.

The incommensurability problem isn't a failure of mathematics — it's deep. The octave and the perfect fifth are both fundamental acoustic relationships, and the fact that they cannot jointly generate a closed finite pitch system is a structural property of logarithms, not a cultural decision.

Harry Partch's music is sometimes described as theatrical rather than purely sonic — the custom instruments are visual objects, and their strangeness signals to the audience that a different acoustic world is in play before the first note sounds.

Microtonality forces you to ask: what is the minimum pitch difference that is perceptually meaningful? The answer depends on timbre, register, duration, and musical context — it's not a single number.

Well temperament, as Bach probably used it, made each key differently coloured — C major had a purity that B major lacked. 'The Well-Tempered Clavier' wasn't arguing for equal temperament; it was arguing that all well-tempered keys are usable, not that they are identical.

The 7-limit in just intonation includes ratios involving 7, giving you intervals like the 7:4 harmonic seventh — significantly flatter than any chord in 12-EDO and with a particular quality that equal temperament simply cannot approximate without obvious beating.

The Arabic quarter-tone isn't half a semitone in the same way a semitone is half a whole tone. The maqam system has its own interval logic, its own grammar of approach and resolution, and quarter-tones are embedded in that grammar — not ornaments on top of it.

Equal temperament solved a real problem — before it, orchestras and ensembles tuned differently in different regions, and ensemble playing across the octave division was a constant practical headache.

The Pythagorean comma is approximately 23.46 cents. For reference, a semitone in equal temperament is 100 cents. So the comma is less than a quarter-tone — perceptible, but only just, at the end of a long chain of perfect fifths.

Partch's 43-tone scale wasn't random — it was derived systematically from the 11-limit, including all ratios up to the 11th harmonic. The result is a pitch-world with intervals that have no equivalents in any equal division of the octave.

Harmonic purity creates a practical asymmetry: string ensembles and unaccompanied voices can tune justly on the fly, adjusting pitch in real time. Fixed-pitch instruments cannot. This asymmetry shapes which instruments are used in which repertoires.

19-EDO has nearly perfect minor thirds and minor sixths — better than 12-EDO — but its major thirds are worse. Every equal division optimises for some just intervals at the cost of others. There is no equal division that is uniformly better than 12-EDO for all intervals.

The fact that we call 12-EDO 'equal' temperament is already ideological. It equalises the error, yes — but the error is still there. 'Equal temperament' sounds like a solved problem. 'Equally distributed impurity' would be more accurate.

Meantone tuning's great thirds came at a cost: modulation was constrained. Certain key relationships were forbidden because the wolf interval lurked at the edge of the available key signatures. Composition was shaped by the tuning system's failure mode.

One thing that's underappreciated about just intonation: when you play a pure fifth, the combined waveform doesn't beat. There's a kind of acoustic stillness that equal-tempered fifths, which beat slowly, don't have. Whether that stillness is musically valuable depends entirely on context.

The maqam system inherited from Persian, Turkish, and Arabic traditions contains modes whose internal intervals resist reduction to any equal octave division currently in common use. Some musicologists argue this is a strength — the intervals are acoustically motivated, not mathematically convenient.

Microtonality in Western art music often sounds jarring to unprepared ears — but the same ear that hears quarter-tones as wrong will hear maqam music as perfectly natural given enough exposure. The 'wrongness' is a calibration artefact, not an acoustic fact.

The classical Indian system uses shruti — 22 microtonal pitch positions within the octave — as the theoretical substrate from which various raga scales draw their notes. The shruti divisions are not equal divisions; they follow just ratios.

Equal temperament collapsed key character — the idea that D minor has a different emotional quality than F# minor — because all keys became acoustically identical. Some composers mourned this. Others found it liberating.

The Pythagorean comma doesn't just create a problem for tuning — it creates a topology. The circle of fifths is a circle precisely because we close it by fudging the last fifth. Without that fudge, it would be an infinite spiral.

Partch is often discussed as an eccentric outsider, but his 43-tone system is rigorously derived from first principles. The eccentricity is in the notation and the instruments, not in the underlying harmonic logic.

If just intonation produces purer intervals, why didn't it win out over equal temperament historically? Because purity and mobility are in direct tension. You can have pure thirds or you can modulate freely — the mathematics will not give you both simultaneously.

The octave division question is really a question about what counts as musically relevant pitch difference. 12-EDO says 100 cents. Some microtonal traditions use 50 cents. Others use 33 cents. The answer is culturally and physically constrained, but not fully determined by either.

Quarter-tones in 24-EDO are exactly 50 cents — precisely between two 12-EDO semitones. But many Arabic maqam intervals that are described as 'quarter-tones' are not 50 cents; they sit at positions that can only be approximated by 24-EDO, not exactly represented.

The wolf interval is philosophically interesting: every regular meantone tuning has exactly one of them, and its position shifts depending on the root of the tuning. You can move it, but you cannot eliminate it — you can only decide which key relationships to sacrifice.

Spectral music, which treats the overtone series as its harmonic foundation, implicitly works with just intonation ratios — it draws its chord structures directly from the integer relationships in the harmonic series. Spectral and microtonal aren't the same thing, but they overlap here.

The syntonic comma — 81:80, approximately 21.5 cents — is the difference between a Pythagorean major third and a pure 5:4 major third. Meantone tuning is literally a strategy for distributing this comma across four fifths so that major thirds come out pure.

Microtonality opens compositional territory that is geometrically larger than 12-EDO — exponentially more pitch classes, more interval categories, more voice-leading possibilities. Whether this larger space is musically useful or simply overwhelming is a genuine open question.

Harry Partch's insistence on just intonation meant that his music could never be transcribed for standard instruments and faithfully realised. This is not a limitation — it's a stance. The music and the instruments are inseparable.

The irreconcilability at the heart of tuning theory isn't a puzzle waiting to be solved — it's a fundamental constraint. Any system of fixed pitches is a choice about which errors to hide, not an escape from error.

Harmonic purity and octave division are pulling in opposite directions: the purer the intervals, the more fixed and non-modulating the pitch world must be. Perfect purity requires an infinite keyboard, or a choir that retunes in real time.
